findings.headline: GDH-PQQ meters show significant interference from icodextrin and maltose
findings.detail: GDH-PQQ glucose meters produce falsely high readings in the presence of icodextrin (mean difference 3.41 ± 1.56 mmol/L) and maltose. This is critical for patients on peritoneal dialysis and highlights the need for FDA-recommended alternatives.

findings.headline: Glucose oxidase method is vulnerable to ascorbic acid interference, which can lead to lower blood glucose readings
findings.detail: The glucose oxidase method involves the enzymatic oxidation of glucose to gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), which is then measured using a peroxidase-coupled reaction. Ascorbic acid is identified as a significant interfering substance that affects the accuracy of glucose measurements using this method, leading to lower readings due to its consumption of hydrogen peroxide.

findings.headline: Hematocrit significantly affects glucose meter accuracy
findings.detail: Hematocrit levels influence glucose readings by 11–12% at normal hematocrit (45%) and up to 30–70% in chronic disease patients. Dynamic electrochemistry and hematocrit correction algorithms improve accuracy across hematocrit ranges.

findings.headline: Fourth-generation biosensors use enzyme-free nanostructured electrodes with improved stability
findings.detail: Fourth-generation biosensors employ enzyme-free technologies with nanostructured electrodes, such as metal nanoparticles, metal oxides, metal alloys, and carbon-based nanoparticles, which enhance sensor stability without requiring glucose oxidase. These sensors do not rely on enzymatic materials for glucose oxidation, instead utilizing non-enzymatic means to directly oxidize glucose. This design contributes to improved stability compared to earlier generations.
